ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A uniformly charged metallic ring of radius $R$ and total charge $q$ is analyzed. The ring is a hollow toroid of thickness $2a$, where $2a \ll R$. The $xy$ plane coincides with the plane of the ring, and the $z$-axis is perpendicular to it. A Taylor expansion formula is provided: $(1+x)^\varepsilon \approx 1 + \varepsilon x + \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon(\varepsilon-1)x^2$, when $|x| \ll 1$. The problem explores the electrostatic potential, forces, and motion of electrons in relation to this charged ring, as well as the ring's properties as a capacitor and its use as an electrostatic lens.

1. A.1 Calculate the electrostatic potential $\Phi(z)$ along the axis of the ring at a $z$ distance from its center (point A in Figure 1).
2. E.1 Find the focal length $f$ of the lens. Assume that $f / v \gg R_0C$, but $d / v$ and $R_0C$ are of the same order of magnitude. Express your answer in terms of the constant $\beta$ from part B and other known quantities.
3. E.2 You will see, that the result for $f$ is similar to that obtained in part C, whereby the value $q$ is substituted with $q_{\text{eff}}$. Find the expression for $q_{\text{eff}}$ in terms of quantities given in formulation of the problem.
4. A.2 Calculate the electrostatic potential $\Phi(z)$ to the lowest non-zero power of $z$, assuming $z \ll R$.
5. An electron (mass $m$ and charge $-e$) is placed at point A (Figure 1, $z \ll R$). What is the force acting on the electron? Looking at the expression of the force, determine the sign of $q$ so that the resulting motion would correspond to oscillations. The moving electron does not influence the charge distribution on the ring.
6. A.4 What is the angular frequency $\omega$ of such harmonic oscillations?
7. B.1 Find the expression for $\beta$. You might need to use the Taylor expansion formula given above.
8. B.2 An electron is placed at point B (Figure 1, $r \ll R$). What is the force acting on the electron?
9. C.1 Determine the focal length $f$ of this lens. Assume that $f \gg d$. Express your answer in terms of the constant $\beta$ from question B.1 and other known quantities. Assume that before reaching the "active region" the electron packet is parallel to the $z$-axis and $r \ll R$. The sign of $q$ is such so that the lens is focusing.
10. C.2 Find $c$. Express your answer in terms of the constant $\beta$ from question B.1 and other known quantities.
11. D.1 Calculate the capacitance $C$ of the ring. Consider that the ring has a finite width $2a$, but remember that $a \ll R$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
$\Phi(z)=\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{R^{2}+z^{2}}}$.
$\Phi(z) \approx \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} R}(1-\frac{z^{2}}{2 R^{2}})$
$F(z)=-\frac{q e}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} R^{3}} z$
$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{q e}{4 \pi m \varepsilon_{0} R^{3}}}$
$\beta=\frac{1}{16 \pi \varepsilon_{0} R^{3}}$
$F(r)=+\frac{q e}{8 \pi \varepsilon_{0} R^{3}} r $
$f=-\frac{E}{e q d \beta}$
$c=-\frac{1}{\frac{e q \beta d}{E}+\frac{1}{b}}$.
$C=\frac{4 \pi^{2} \varepsilon_{0} R}{\ln (\frac{8 R}{a})}$
$f=-\frac{E}{e C V_{0} d \beta}$
$q_{\text{eff}}=C V_{0}$

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a circuit used for charging/discharging an annular conductor. On the left there is a voltage source labeled V0, and there is a double-throw switch; the output terminal of the switch is connected through resistor R0 to the circular ring conductor on the right. Beside the ring is labeled C, indicating the capacitance of this ring as a capacitor. The figure also draws another grounded/reference-terminal switch position, so this circuit structure supports connecting the ring through R0 to voltage V0 to undergo RC charging, and after a sufficiently long time the charge on the ring tends to C V0. Reasoning: Since the ring is a hollow thin ring of radius R and thickness 2a, with a << R, it can first be treated as a uniformly charged circular line of radius R, let k=1/(4 pi epsilon0). A.1: A point on the axis at distance z from the center of the circle has the same distance to any charge element on the ring, all being sqrt(R^2+z^2). Therefore dPhi=k dq/sqrt(R^2+z^2), integrating over the whole ring gives Phi(z)=k q/sqrt(R^2+z^2). A.2: When z << R, Phi(z)=kq/R (1+z^2/R^2)^(-1/2). Using the given Taylor formula, take epsilon=-1/2 and x=z^2/R^2, only the lowest nonzero z-order term needs to be retained, obtaining Phi(z)≈kq/R [1 - z^2/(2R^2)]. A.3/A.4: The axial electric field E_z=-dPhi/dz. From the near-axis potential, dPhi/dz≈-kq z/R^3, so E_z≈kq z/R^3. The electron charge is -e, therefore F_z=(-e)E_z= -k q e z/R^3. If when z>0 the force needs to point toward -z to be a restoring force, then q>0 is required. The equation of motion is m z¨=-(kqe/R^3)z, therefore omega=sqrt(kqe/(mR^3))=sqrt(qe/(4 pi m epsilon0 R^3)). B.1: In the plane of the ring, at point B with radial distance r from the center, take rho=r/R. The line-charge potential is Phi(r)=k q/(2 pi) integral_0^{2pi} dphi / sqrt(R^2+r^2-2Rr cos phi)=kq/R <(1+rho^2-2rho cos phi)^(-1/2)>. Expanding to rho^2: 1 - 1/2(rho^2-2rho cos phi)+3/8(rho^2-2rho cos phi)^2. After retaining to second order it is 1+rho cos phi -rho^2/2 +(3/2)rho^2 cos^2 phi. Averaging over phi, <cos phi>=0, <cos^2 phi>=1/2, so the average value is 1+rho^2/4. Therefore Phi(r)=kq/R + kq r^2/(4R^3). If written as Phi(r)=Phi(0)+q beta r^2, then beta=k/(4R^3)=1/(16 pi epsilon0 R^3). B.2: The radial electric field E_r=-dPhi/dr=-2q beta r. The force on the electron is F_r=(-e)E_r=2eq beta r=qe r/(8 pi epsilon0 R^3), in the +r direction (when q>0). C.1: In the thin-lens region of length d, approximate the radial force as a constant small impulse. The electron velocity is v, and kinetic energy E=mv^2/2. The transverse slope change Delta r'=F_r d/(m v^2)=(2eq beta r)d/(m v^2)=(e q beta d/E)r. The thin-lens convention is Delta r'=-r/f, therefore -1/f=e q beta d/E, so f=-E/(e q d beta). When focusing, f>0, so q should take the sign that makes the denominator negative, namely q<0. C.2: If the ray incident at the lens is equivalent before the lens to coming from a point at distance b, then the incident slope can be written as r/b. The emergent slope is r/b+(e q beta d/E)r. Let it intersect the axis at distance c after the lens, r+c[r/b+(e q beta d/E)r]=0, so c=-1/(e q beta d/E+1/b). D.1: For a thin circular conductor tube, the self-potential is known to be approximately V=q ln(8R/a)/(4 pi^2 epsilon0 R). Therefore C=q/V=4 pi^2 epsilon0 R/ln(8R/a). E.1/E.2: The attached circuit shows that the ring is connected through R0 to the voltage source V0 and charges as capacitance C. Under the given approximation, the lens action can use the same thin-lens result as in part C, only needing to replace the fixed charge q with the effective charge q_eff. After the RC process, the effective charge is q_eff=C V0, therefore f=-E/(e C V0 d beta), and q_eff=C V0.

ready3_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: $\Phi(z)=\frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{R^{2}+z^{2}}}$. $\Phi(z) \approx \frac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} R}(1-\frac{z^{2}}{2 R^{2}})$ $F(z)=-\frac{q e}{4 \pi \varepsilon_{0} R^{3}} z$ $\omega=\sqrt{\frac{q e}{4 \pi m \varepsilon_{0} R^{3}}}$ $\beta=\frac{1}{16 \pi \varepsilon_{0} R^{3}}$ $F(r)=+\frac{q e}{8 \pi \varepsilon_{0} R^{3}} r $ $f=-\frac{E}{e q d \beta}$ $c=-\frac{1}{\frac{e q \beta d}{E}+\frac{1}{b}}$. $C=\frac{4 \pi^{2} \varepsilon_{0} R}{\ln (\frac{8 R}{a})}$ $f=-\frac{E}{e C V_{0} d \beta}$ $q_{\text{eff}}=C V_{0}$
ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The attached figure shows a circuit used for charging/discharging an annular conductor. On the left there is a voltage source labeled V0, and there is a double-throw switch; the output terminal of the switch is connected through resistor R0 to the circular ring conductor on the right. Beside the ring is labeled C, indicating the capacitance of this ring as a capacitor. The figure also draws another grounded/reference-terminal switch position, so this circuit structure supports connecting the ring through R0 to voltage V0 to undergo RC charging, and after a sufficiently long time the charge on the ring tends to C V0.

Reasoning: Since the ring is a hollow thin ring of radius R and thickness 2a, with a << R, it can first be treated as a uniformly charged circular line of radius R, let k=1/(4 pi epsilon0).

A.1: A point on the axis at distance z from the center of the circle has the same distance to any charge element on the ring, all being sqrt(R^2+z^2). Therefore dPhi=k dq/sqrt(R^2+z^2), integrating over the whole ring gives Phi(z)=k q/sqrt(R^2+z^2).

A.2: When z << R, Phi(z)=kq/R (1+z^2/R^2)^(-1/2). Using the given Taylor formula, take epsilon=-1/2 and x=z^2/R^2, only the lowest nonzero z-order term needs to be retained, obtaining Phi(z)≈kq/R [1 - z^2/(2R^2)].

A.3/A.4: The axial electric field E_z=-dPhi/dz. From the near-axis potential, dPhi/dz≈-kq z/R^3, so E_z≈kq z/R^3. The electron charge is -e, therefore F_z=(-e)E_z= -k q e z/R^3. If when z>0 the force needs to point toward -z to be a restoring force, then q>0 is required. The equation of motion is m z¨=-(kqe/R^3)z, therefore omega=sqrt(kqe/(mR^3))=sqrt(qe/(4 pi m epsilon0 R^3)).

B.1: In the plane of the ring, at point B with radial distance r from the center, take rho=r/R. The line-charge potential is Phi(r)=k q/(2 pi) integral_0^{2pi} dphi / sqrt(R^2+r^2-2Rr cos phi)=kq/R <(1+rho^2-2rho cos phi)^(-1/2)>. Expanding to rho^2: 1 - 1/2(rho^2-2rho cos phi)+3/8(rho^2-2rho cos phi)^2. After retaining to second order it is 1+rho cos phi -rho^2/2 +(3/2)rho^2 cos^2 phi. Averaging over phi, <cos phi>=0, <cos^2 phi>=1/2, so the average value is 1+rho^2/4. Therefore Phi(r)=kq/R + kq r^2/(4R^3). If written as Phi(r)=Phi(0)+q beta r^2, then beta=k/(4R^3)=1/(16 pi epsilon0 R^3).

B.2: The radial electric field E_r=-dPhi/dr=-2q beta r. The force on the electron is F_r=(-e)E_r=2eq beta r=qe r/(8 pi epsilon0 R^3), in the +r direction (when q>0).

C.1: In the thin-lens region of length d, approximate the radial force as a constant small impulse. The electron velocity is v, and kinetic energy E=mv^2/2. The transverse slope change Delta r'=F_r d/(m v^2)=(2eq beta r)d/(m v^2)=(e q beta d/E)r. The thin-lens convention is Delta r'=-r/f, therefore -1/f=e q beta d/E, so f=-E/(e q d beta). When focusing, f>0, so q should take the sign that makes the denominator negative, namely q<0.

C.2: If the ray incident at the lens is equivalent before the lens to coming from a point at distance b, then the incident slope can be written as r/b. The emergent slope is r/b+(e q beta d/E)r. Let it intersect the axis at distance c after the lens, r+c[r/b+(e q beta d/E)r]=0, so c=-1/(e q beta d/E+1/b).

D.1: For a thin circular conductor tube, the self-potential is known to be approximately V=q ln(8R/a)/(4 pi^2 epsilon0 R). Therefore C=q/V=4 pi^2 epsilon0 R/ln(8R/a).

E.1/E.2: The attached circuit shows that the ring is connected through R0 to the voltage source V0 and charges as capacitance C. Under the given approximation, the lens action can use the same thin-lens result as in part C, only needing to replace the fixed charge q with the effective charge q_eff. After the RC process, the effective charge is q_eff=C V0, therefore f=-E/(e C V0 d beta), and q_eff=C V0.
